implementation_notes: Moq makes the programming of canned answers the path of least resistance: new Mock<IWarehouse>() builds the double, Setup(x => x.HasInventory("Talisker", 50)).Returns(false) states the answer with a compile-checked lambda (no string method names), and stub.Object implements the interface through a generated proxy driven by LINQ expression trees. Microsoft's unit-testing guidance shows exactly this shape for a clock stub, and notes that when no mocking library is allowed the same double is written as a class deriving from the client type and overriding the members the test calls - that hand-written class is what Setup/Returns replaces. Keep the default loose mode and do not call Verify when the double is a stub: verification is the mock reading of the same object.
pitfalls: Setups must be configured before stub.Object is handed to the SUT; a later Setup only affects calls that have not happened yet.
Strict mocks throw on any call that was not set up, so a missing canned answer fails as a complaint about the double; stubs belong in the default loose mode.

Mocking a concrete type requires the member to be virtual or abstract; sealed types, statics and non-virtual members cannot be stubbed this way and need an interface you own or a hand-written subclass.

variants.name: Hand-written stub class (no mocking library)
variants.idiom_name: test class implementing the collaborator interface with fixed returns
variants.implementation_notes: Without a mocking library the stub is a small class implementing the collaborator interface (or deriving from the testable client and overriding the members the test calls, the pattern Microsoft documents for Azure SDK clients), with the canned values hard-coded or set in the constructor. It needs no package, is fully compile-checked, and is preferable where the double must also carry real behaviour or where the team bans dynamic proxies; Microsoft Fakes generates the same kind of stub class when the interface is large. Use it when the mock framework's loose defaults would answer for methods you did not intend to program, and switch to an interface-first design so the class stays implementable.
pitfalls: Implementing the whole interface means the stub breaks whenever the interface grows; keep the collaborator interface narrow at the consumer side.
A stub holding mutable state (a counter, captured arguments) is copied or shared between tests unless it is re-created per test.
Sealed classes and static members cannot be stubbed this way either - they need an interface, a wrapper, or a shim.
